title: The Roster Trap: Why Longer Christmas Trading Hours Don't Always Mean a More Profitable Retailer
excerpt: Extending Christmas trading hours feels like the obvious move for retailers. The pattern we see is that the newest hours often cost more in wages than they return in margin, right when it matters most.
content:
Retailers across Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria are finalising their Christmas rosters this week, stretching trading hours into the evening and adding casual staff to cover Boxing Day and the January sales rush. A fuller trading calendar looks like an obvious win heading into the six busiest weeks of the retail year.

The pattern we see across owner-led bricks and mortar retailers is less straightforward. Revenue climbs reliably when the doors stay open longer, but profit does not always climb at the same rate, because the wage cost of the extra hours rises faster than most rosters account for. Public holiday loadings, casual penalty rates and the extra supervision a bigger trading week demands all land in the same six weeks the business is counting on to carry its year.

None of this means the longer hours are the wrong call. It means the decision deserves the same scrutiny as any other investment the business makes, because not every hour on the roster earns its keep at the same rate.

Not Every Trading Hour Carries the Same Margin

Sales density is never flat across a trading day. The late Saturday afternoon rush and the last ninety minutes before close on a weeknight behave very differently, and the hour that generates the least revenue per dollar of wage cost is rarely the hour an owner would guess without checking. When a store extends its hours to capture extra Christmas trade, the new hours are usually the thinnest ones, the early morning slot before school drop off or the closing stretch after most shoppers have already finished. Revenue from those hours is real. Whether it covers the wage cost of staffing them, including any penalty or casual loading that applies, is a separate question, and one most retailers answer by instinct rather than by the numbers.

The Roster Looks Fuller. The Cost Per Hour Just Moved As Well.

Boxing Day and New Year's Day both attract public holiday penalty rates, and casual loading sits on top of that for any team member without guaranteed hours. Many retailers build this year's Christmas roster from last year's figures, adjusted for a few extra shifts, without re-checking whether award rates moved during the year or whether last year's roster was ever actually profitable hour for hour. The gap between the roster that was planned and the wage bill that lands usually only becomes visible in the January pay run, well after the decisions that created it were made.

The extra supervision a longer trading week requires compounds this. A store open for an extra two or three hours a day across December does not just need the shop floor covered, it needs a keyholder, someone accountable for cash handling and someone who can manage a queue when the store is at its busiest. That additional layer of cost rarely appears as its own line item, which is part of why it is so easy to miss until the margin for the month comes in lower than the revenue suggested it should.

This is rarely visible in the headline numbers. December revenue is the strongest month of the year for most retailers, and a strong top line makes it easy to assume the result underneath is proportionally strong too. It is only when gross margin is checked against the same month last year, rather than against revenue alone, that the gap this extra labour cost creates becomes visible. By the time the January pay run lands and the real wage cost is tallied, the trading month that looked the most successful on paper can turn out to be one of the thinner months for margin.

What to Track Instead of Simply Whether the Doors Are Open

The useful number is not total trading hours or total December revenue. It is revenue, or better, contribution margin, measured per labour hour for each shift on the roster, compared against the direct cost of staffing that shift including whatever loading applies. Once that number exists by shift and by day, it becomes obvious which hours are genuinely adding to the result and which are being carried along because closing early feels like giving something up. A workforce capacity and utilisation review builds exactly this picture, measuring throughput and unit labour cost shift by shift rather than relying on a monthly profit and loss statement that only shows the average across the whole trading week.

This is a pattern that is almost impossible to see mid season and straightforward to see once the hours are laid against the margin on paper. It is also the kind of structured review a fractional CFO brings to an owner-led retail business in the quieter weeks of January, while the data from this Christmas is still fresh and next year's roster is still a blank page. If this Christmas's trading hours have never been tested against what they actually return, a conversation before the next roster is built is a reasonable place to start.

faqs.q: Why doesn't a longer Christmas trading week always mean more retail profit?
faqs.a: Because not every extra trading hour earns the same margin. The hours added to capture extra Christmas trade are usually the thinnest ones in the day, and the wage cost of staffing them, including any penalty or casual loading, does not automatically track the revenue they bring in. Revenue can rise while the margin on those specific hours barely covers what it costs to staff them.

faqs.q: How much do public holiday penalty rates add to Christmas retail wage costs in Australia?
faqs.a: Penalty rates for Boxing Day and New Year's Day trading, layered with casual loading for any team member without guaranteed hours, can lift the cost of those specific shifts well above a standard trading day. The exact loading depends on the award and classification, but the pattern across owner-led retailers is that the roster is often built from last year's figures without checking whether award rates moved, which leaves the real cost higher than planned.

faqs.q: What is unit labour cost and why does it matter for a retail Christmas roster?
faqs.a: Unit labour cost is the wage cost of a shift measured against the revenue or margin that shift actually generates, rather than against the trading day as a whole. It matters because a store's average margin for December can look healthy while specific shifts, often the newly added ones, are barely breaking even once penalty and casual loading are included. Measuring by shift rather than by month is what reveals this.

faqs.q: Should a small retailer open on Boxing Day and New Year's Day?
faqs.a: That depends on whether the revenue those days generate clears the penalty rate and casual loading cost of staffing them, which varies by location and by store. Some retailers find Boxing Day comfortably justifies the cost, while New Year's Day trade is thinner and barely covers it. The only reliable way to know is to measure each trading day on its own numbers rather than assume both days behave the same way.

faqs.q: How can a retailer tell which Christmas trading hours are actually profitable?
faqs.a: By comparing the contribution margin generated in each shift against the direct cost of staffing it, including whatever loading applies, rather than relying on the total revenue or average margin for the month. Once that number exists shift by shift, the hours that are genuinely adding to the result become clear, as do the ones being carried along because closing early feels like a concession.

faqs.q: What does a Workforce Capacity and Utilisation Review look like for a retail business?
faqs.a: It is a structured review of how staffing hours translate into revenue and margin, measuring throughput and unit labour cost shift by shift rather than relying on a monthly profit and loss statement that averages everything together. For a retailer, that means knowing which trading hours, including the ones added for Christmas, are carrying the result and which are not. The workforce capacity and utilisation review is built for exactly this question.

faqs.q: When should a retailer review this year's Christmas trading hours before planning next year's roster?
faqs.a: The best time is January, while the data from the trading peak just finished is still complete and specific, rather than waiting until next November when the same roster decisions get repeated from memory. Reviewing contribution margin by shift straight after the peak, while the figures are fresh, is the kind of discipline a fractional CFO brings to an owner-led retail business between seasons.
